extracted.intended_audience: scientists, academics, and educated readers evaluating or selecting scientific books and textbooks (e.g., historians of science, agricultural teachers, geologists, ecologists, physicists, biologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for evaluating scholarly/scientific books (monographs, textbooks, handbooks) across natural-science fields, emphasizing scholarship, clarity, methodology, pedagogy, accuracy and up-to-dateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly, unbiased treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should be a scholarly contribution, telling the story (or presenting the subject) without bias and dispassionately, in the light of all available information, and written in the true spirit of the discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example praise: 'the story of his life is here told without bias, dispassionately, and in the light of all available information, and the result is an eminently readable monograph written in the true spirit of history.' Anti-pattern: partisan or polemical accounts that ignore contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and completeness of narrative and use of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical or survey accounts should trace developments clearly and be pieced together from appropriate primary and secondary sources (manorial records, sayings, illuminated MSS., etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice: use a wide range of contemporary and archival sources to produce a continuous and clear account. Anti-pattern: patchy treatment that omits relevant documentary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insider knowledge and vivid reporting of recent events
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating recent or contemporary episodes, authors who have inside knowledge and freedom to relate events can present vivid, authoritative accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive example: chapters on war farming praised for 'double advantage of inside knowledge and of freedom... and he tells the story vividly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for intended audience and pedagogical utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Books aimed at students or teachers should be simply written, accessible without extensive background, unbiassed, and include pedagogical features (stimulating content, suitable introductions to larger works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit recommendation: 'Teachers of agriculture generally will welcome... they can place in the hands of their students.' Good illustrations and readability increase pedagogical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and appropriateness of illustrations and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations should be excellent and well chosen to demonstrate contrasts (e.g., older vs newer implements) and reinforce text; examples should be representative and didactically useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive note: illustrations 'show, side by side, the older and the newer types... and afford admirable demonstrations of the great changes.' Anti-pattern: irrelevant or poorly chosen figures that confuse rather than clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and clarity of definitions and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Key technical terms and classificatory phrases must be defined in satisfactory, non-confusing ways (e.g., definitions of 'epigenetic' and 'syngenetic' should avoid excluding natural cases and should support clear understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique example: the reviewer finds the author's basal definitions 'by no means satisfactory' because they exclude certain deposits and create confusion. Good practice: definitions that align with sounder views and lead to clearer understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural, comprehensible classification (avoid excessive subdivision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification schemes should follow broad lines where natural groupings exist; minute subdivisions based on small differences often hinder understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'minute subdivision of mineral veins based upon differences, and sometimes small differences, in their mineral contents' causes confusion. Recommendation: fewer typical examples and simpler classification, with references for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative selection of examples (not exhaustive listing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer quoting typical, illustrative examples and giving references to other cases rather than attempting encyclopedic descriptions of every occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer advice: 'more care will have to be devoted to classification and to the discussion of the modes of formation of the deposits, and fewer examples, and those only typical ones, must be quoted, references to descriptions of others being generally sufficient.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy (geography, citations, omissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual correctness in geographical statements and completeness (avoid notable omissions) is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning example: 'various mistakes in geography, which should have been avoided; for example, the Sierra de Ronda is said to be on the Portuguese coast, and Leadville in England!' Also note notable omissions of important deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level for audience: beginner-safe vs expert reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should match scope and depth to the intended audience — texts intended for students should be safe and clear for beginners; highly detailed, reference works may be useful only for experienced specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer distinction: the work 'may be of use for reference to the experienced mining geologist... but it is scarcely a safe book to place in the hands of a beginner.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Up-to-date literature review and international awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must cite and incorporate recent, relevant literature (including non-local/international work) so their accounts reflect current knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: 'gives no references to any non-German work of a later date than 1912' — remedy: survey recent English and American journals to capture developments and useful facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical rigor and reporting of variability/significance
rubrics_metrics.description: When quantitative counts or measurements are presented, authors should report statistical variation (duplicates, ranges, significance) so readers can judge the reliability of observed differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example critique: numbers of organisms per mm^3 given without information on variation between duplicate samples — 'the reader... is at a great disadvantage if he is not told just what is the degree of significance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological detail and practical techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Handbooks on methods should include sufficient detail of physical/chemical techniques (e.g., calcimeters, freezing-point depression, electrical or colorimetric pH methods, nitrate determinations) to guide practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission critique: no description of modern calcimeters or methods for hydrogen-ion concentration; recommendation: include cross-disciplinary technique details so biological investigators can apply them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical structuring of fundamentals and clear statement of laws/principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts should present foundational laws and principles in a clear, logically coherent way (e.g., thermodynamics should open with agreed statements of the First and Second Laws rather than a tendentious preamble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer reference: Carathéodory's formulation praised for logical manner; suggestion: remove implied assumptions and structure presentation to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching general concepts by misleading special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not introduce general concepts through special-case examples that risk leaving incorrect impressions about their generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: introducing absolute temperature via the perfect gas may leave students with the idea that temperature is linked to perfect gases; better to justify general concepts in the general case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrative examples and up-to-date developments
rubrics_metrics.description: Include numerous illustrative examples and incorporate recent theoretical or experimental developments (e.g., modern solution theory, equations of state, X-ray crystal structure findings) appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive: Planck's book praised for 'numerous illustrative examples from physical chemistry' and added material on theory of solutions and solids; negative: very brief treatment of X-ray crystallography in mineralogy (only ~one page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to statistical methods and observer/personal equation
rubrics_metrics.description: When employing statistical approaches, authors should discuss limitations, the 'personal equation', and the potential for spurious accuracy arising from method or interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer: 'statistical methods... results so obtained are often by no means free from the personal equation, and hence often have a spurious appearance of accuracy to which attention is rightly drawn.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary sensibility and caution about anthropomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary treatments (e.g., combining music and biology) should bring relevant expertise but avoid over-anthropomorphising natural phenomena; representation methods should aim for phrasing and dominant features rather than unattainable exact imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bird-song notation should focus on 'accuracy of phrasing combined with a fair approximation to the succession of dominant vowels and consonants'; warn: 'some danger of too anthropomorphic ways of thinking.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis of scattered literature and systematic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuable texts often assemble and synthesise work previously scattered across many sources, presenting systematic analytical and synthetical parts (history/bibliography, analysis, practical formulae and experimental evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive example: Dr. Salmon's book consolidates much scattered work, gives analytical discussion and practical formulae, and suggests directions for future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate geographic and topical scope (balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should ensure their geographical/examples scope matches the intended audience and reflect worldwide significance rather than over-concentrating on a single country unless explicitly targeted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique example: 'General Economic Geology' 'is written primarily for an American public' with most examples from America and little mention of equally important occurrences elsewhere; adjust or state scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of useful supplementary materials (bibliography, maps, diagrams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Helpful additions include excellent bibliographies, maps, diagrams, half-tone blocks, and other illustrative supplements that enhance the book's utility for study and reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer praise: 'the addition of an excellent bibliography... text throughout is plentifully supplemented with maps, diagrams, and half-tone blocks.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernization of terminology and avoidance of antiquated nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks should update obsolete terms and adopt scientifically current nomenclature (e.g., moving away from antiquated symmetry descriptors toward elements of symmetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mineralogy text praised for reducing use of 'hemihedral' and 'tetartohedral' as antiquated and instead referring to definite elements of symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit recommendations for future research and open questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Good technical monographs often point out pressing unanswered questions and suggest directions for future experimental or theoretical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dr. Salmon identifies 'the most pressing point for future research... the degree of imperfection common in practical direction-fixed ends' and the reviewer regards such suggestions as carrying weight.
